exam: A 45‑year‑old man with BMI 32 kg/m² presents with resistant hypertension and loud snoring. What is your next diagnostic step? — Use STOP‑Bang; if high, arrange portable oximetry or polysomnography.
Explain how the Apnoea‑Hypopnoea Index determines OSA severity. — Count apnoeas + hypopnoeas per hour; thresholds 5‑14 mild, 15‑29 moderate, ≥30 severe.
A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy develops OSA. Which HIV‑related factor increases risk? — Cervical lymphadenopathy and fat redistribution enlarge neck circumference.
Why is CPAP contraindicated in a patient with untreated pneumothorax? — Positive pressure can expand the pneumothorax, causing tension physiology.
Describe two bedside maneuvers to assess upper airway obstruction risk. — Measure neck circumference >40 cm; perform Mallampati assessment.
A patient with OSA is started on CPAP but continues to be sleepy. What should you consider? — Poor mask fit, inadequate pressure, or comorbid depression; reassess adherence and titrate pressure.
How does untreated OSA contribute to cardiovascular mortality? — Intermittent hypoxia triggers sympathetic activation, endothelial dysfunction, and arrhythmogenesis.
Differentiate OSA from obesity hypoventilation syndrome in a morbidly obese patient. — OSA shows episodic apnoeas with normal daytime CO₂; OHS has chronic hypercapnia and daytime hypoventilation.
ai.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder of upper airway collapse during sleep, causing intermittent hypoxia and fragmented sleep. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical scoring and limited investigations.

sections.p: OSA occurs when pharyngeal muscles relax excessively during sleep, leading to partial or complete airway obstruction. It is prevalent in adults with obesity, craniofacial abnormalities, and certain infections common in the tropics.

Risk factors: obesity, neck circumference >40 cm, male sex, HIV‑related lymphadenopathy, TB scarring, craniofacial malformations
sections.p: Diagnosis uses the Apnoea‑Hypopnoea Index (AHI): number of apnoeas plus hypopnoeas per hour of sleep. Severity: mild 5‑14, moderate 15‑29, severe ≥30 events/h.

sections.p: Patients present with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, nocturnal choking, and excessive daytime sleepiness. In low‑resource hospitals, look for hypertension, resistant hypertension, and cardiac arrhythmias as clues.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide airway support and lifestyle measures. In low‑resource settings, CPAP may be limited; alternatives include positional therapy and weight reduction.
